text:
**Recommendation: a split, routed by a per-client consent flag. Contracts from consenting clients go to a hosted API; contracts from non-consenting clients (and any with unknown consent status) are summarised on one small local machine running an open-weight model. Default to local when in doubt.** Start with local-only for everyone for the first month while you build the consent register and quality checks, then switch consenting clients to the API only if the local summaries fall short or the day-a-week person is spending too much time on the local setup. A single hosted API for everything is not an option, because it would send non-consenting clients' contract text to a third party, which your agreements forbid. Local-only for everything is viable at this volume, so the API is an optimisation, not a necessity.

**Why this shape.** The consent constraint is a hard rule, not a cost trade-off, so it dictates the routing: the data's permission status decides where it goes, not the model's quality. A split lets consenting clients get the stronger hosted models while refusing clients stay fully in-house. It also keeps the design simple for a non-engineer: one flag, two paths, same summary template. Before any consenting client's contract goes to an API, check the vendor's terms: use a business or API tier with no training on your data, short or zero retention, and a data processing agreement. Confirm that your clients' consent wording covers a subprocessor, not just 'a third party' in the abstract. If it doesn't, get the consent letter reworded.

**Cost model (assumptions visible).** Volume: 300 contracts a month at an average of about 35 pages, roughly 500 tokens a page, so about 17,500 tokens a contract and 5.25M input tokens a month. Summaries of about 1,000 output tokens each give 0.3M output tokens. Assume a 50/50 consent split as a planning case, which is a guess you should replace with your real register. API path, 150 contracts: 2.6M input and 0.15M output tokens. At mid-tier pricing of roughly $3 per million input and $15 per million output tokens, that is about $8 plus $2, so about $10 a month. Even if long contracts need a two-pass approach (chunk summaries, then a merge) and you triple the token use, it stays under $30. Budget $50 to cover retries and testing. Local path, 150 contracts: one machine with a 24 GB GPU or a 64 GB unified-memory Mac, about $2,000 to $2,500 all-in, amortised over 36 months is roughly $55 to $70 a month. Add about $10 to $15 a month for electricity and $0 for open-weight models. Total in the planning case: about $70 hardware plus $15 power plus $50 API, so roughly $135 a month, leaving about $165 of headroom. Worst case, with every client refusing, the cost is hardware plus power, about $85, and the local machine must then handle all 300 contracts. At roughly 5 minutes per long contract with chunking, that is about 25 hours of machine time a month, which is easily feasible, even on a slower setup. Best case, with every client consenting, you could skip the hardware, but keeping it is cheap insurance because consent can be withdrawn. Note that I have not priced staff time: the day a week is already allocated, but it is the scarcest resource in this plan.

**Handling non-consenting clients.** The register of consent is the control that matters most. Keep a simple spreadsheet or a field in your document system: client, consent yes/no/unknown, date, who recorded it, link to the written consent. Unknown means no. The routing step should be mechanical, ideally a folder structure (consented/ and restricted/) so a person cannot accidentally upload a restricted file to the API path. Restricted files are processed only on the local machine, which has no outbound upload tooling, and its logs and outputs stay on the firm's network. Review the register quarterly and whenever a client changes their position, and treat a withdrawn consent as an incident: stop sending, and ask the vendor about deletion if retention applies.

**Checking quality before anyone relies on a summary.** Treat summaries as a triage aid, not a substitute for reading, until evidence says otherwise. First, build a test set: 30 to 40 past contracts spanning short and long, simple and messy, both consent categories, each with a summary written or approved by a lawyer or senior colleague. Run both the local and API paths on them and score the results against a fixed checklist: parties, term, fees and payment terms, termination and renewal, liability caps and indemnities, governing law, unusual clauses. Mark each item as correct, missing, or wrong, and track 'wrong' separately because confident errors are worse than omissions. Set a pass bar in advance, for example no wrong statements on key terms in 95 percent of test contracts and 90 percent recall of listed items. Second, in production, require every summary to cite page or clause references so a reader can verify quickly, and have a human spot-check a random 10 percent (about 30 a month, perhaps two hours of work) plus every contract above a value threshold or flagged high-risk. Log the error rate monthly. Third, tell users plainly that a summary can omit things, and that anything driving a decision, such as signing, a dispute or a renewal, needs the source read.

**What would change the recommendation, and how you'd notice.** (1) Consent rates: if nearly all clients consent, drop the local machine, or if nearly all refuse, drop the API; notice via the register, reviewed quarterly. (2) Local quality: if the local model fails the test-set bar on long contracts, options are a larger local machine (around $4,000 to $6,000, or $110 to $170 a month amortised, which still fits if the API share is small), or seeking consent from more clients; notice via the monthly spot-check error rate. (3) Volume: tripling to about 900 contracts a month would raise the API bill to roughly $30 to $150 and local run time to about 75 hours a month; notice via monthly counts, and revisit if API spend passes about $150 or the local queue runs more than a few days behind. (4) Model prices or vendor terms: a price rise of several times, or a change in retention or training terms, should trigger re-review; assign someone to read vendor notices and check the invoice monthly. (5) Maintenance burden: if the day a week is consistently consumed by fixing the local setup rather than checking quality, that is a signal to simplify, which might mean a managed private deployment, if budget allows, or tighter scope. (6) Client agreement changes: new contract wording on subprocessors or AI use overrides everything above.
